Background

Chronic Absenteeism
• Chronic absenteeism (students missing 15 or more days of
 school in a year) has long been a problem in America’s schools.
• In a study conducted by the United States Department of
 Education, in 2015-16, over 7 million students were chronically
 absent on one or more occasions.
• That’s 16 percent of the student population.
• Since the pandemic, concern about chronic absenteeism has
 only grown.

 3

Data
• Attendance data from 2021-2022 and 2022-2023 was supplied by RIDE for
 analysis with RICAS data
• Attendance data supplied included student SASID, District, School,
 Attendance Days Total, Total Days Absent, and a Chronically Absent Flag
• No data was included indicating calendar dates of absences.
• Attendance data was merged with RICAS data to derive summary analyses
 associated with chronic absenteeism.
• Note: Student characteristics (e.g., grade attended, demographics, etc.)
 come from the RICAS data.
• Attendance data covered almost all students with RICAS scores with less than
 2% of students not having attendance data after merging.

Frequencies
• As the data clearly show, chronic absenteeism occurs in Rhode Island at
 elevated rates.
 • In 2021-2022, nearly 3 in 10 students were classified as having an
 instance of chronic absenteeism.
 • In 2022-2023 chronic absenteeism rates dropped slightly above 20%
• The results for Providence school district are even higher.
• We next investigate RICAS performance of these students and attempt to
 tease out the impact of chronic absenteeism on rates of learning.

Achievement Summaries
• The data show a consistent pattern across both years with students who
 were chronically absent demonstrating much lower levels of achievement
 than their non-chronically absent counterparts.
• It would be a mistake to conclude that chronic absenteeism causes this
 lower achievement (this group may be lower achieving to begin with).
• To try and further tease out the effects of chronic absenteeism on learning,
 we next compare the two groups on growth.
 • Because growth conditions on prior achievement, this goes some way to
 dealing with the confounding of achievement and group membership.
 • We utilize cohort referenced SGPs as we are interested in a difference
 between groups.

Growth Summaries
• There are moderate differences between the growth of students who were
 chronically absent from those who were not in both ELA and mathematics
 across all grades.
• Demographic subgroup analyses were conducted to see whether
 interactions with student growth were observed (Free Reduced Lunch status
 results are presented). In general, impacts on growth were fairly consistent
 across subgroups.
• One possible confounding explanation in the above analyses is that the
 group of student who were chronically absent demonstrated slower
 learning (even if not chronically absent) than their comparison group.
• In the last analyses we use students as their own controls to exam the
 impact of chronic absenteeism on student growth.

Conclusions
• Chronic absenteeism is a wide-spread phenomenon in the Rhode Island
 education system.
• Students who are chronically absent tend to be lower achieving that non-
 chronically absent students.
• Examination of student growth over two years shows modest to moderate
 impact on SGPs.
 • Mean SGPs for chronically absent are, for most grades and content areas
 about 4 to 6 points lower than those not chronically absent.
 • When looked at longitudinally, growth decreased/increased modestly for
 those switching between not chronically absent to chronically absent (and
 vice-versa) in 2021-2022 and 2022-2023
• Though not a part of these analyses, it would be worth while to investigate the
 impact of assessment outcomes based upon the proximity of the chronic
 absence to testing time.
